title: Helio Insurance - Procurement/Legal: retention terms + compliance reporting pack deliverables
summary: Helio Procurement/Legal reviewed contract language for Redwood’s Retention Controls and the baseline Compliance Reporting Pack. Helio requested (a) explicit retention defaults and configurable TTL ranges by data class, (b) definition of purge semantics and a “legal hold” exception process, (c) report-pack delivery SLA/timeline and what is included vs. roadmap, (d) assurance around data residency and audit-log export completeness, and (e) clarifications on whether Redwood stores prompts/completions and for how long. Redwood walked through planned deliverables: retention policy controls (request/response logs, audit logs, traces/metrics) and an on-demand evidence package including retention export + audit log coverage summary + RBAC/access summary. Parties aligned to exchange redlines and to provide a customer-facing sample report pack by end of week, with a target initial delivery in the next product phase for Helio’s pilot.
topics: Compliance Reporting Pack baseline: contents, format, and versioning
Retention controls: data classes, TTL defaults, and per-tenant configuration
Purge semantics: deletion jobs, verification metrics, and idempotency
Legal hold / incident hold: approvals, audit trail, and scope
Data residency/region summary in the report pack
Audit log exports: event-type coverage, filters, and time-windowed exports
Contract language: SLAs, timelines, and limitations
next_steps: Redwood to send Helio a sample Compliance Reporting Pack (MVP template) and a one-page description of included sections by 2025-03-07.
Helio to send procurement/legal redlines on retention and reporting deliverables by 2025-03-10.
Redwood to confirm proposed contractual language for legal hold and incident hold workflow (who can request, approval matrix, notification) after internal review.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up with Helio security to validate the audit log event coverage list and any Helio-specific evidence checklist items.
action_items: Olga Petrov: Provide a customer-ready outline of the baseline Compliance Reporting Pack (sections + data sources + export formats) (due 2025-03-07).
Sofia Mendes: Draft contract addendum language for retention configuration + purge semantics + legal hold exception (due 2025-03-10).
Naomi Feldman: Confirm product timeline assumptions for report-pack generation and what can be delivered during Helio pilot vs GA (due 2025-03-07).
Mei Chen (Helio): Share Helio’s internal evidence checklist / SOC2-style control mapping expectations (due 2025-03-10).
transcript:
Meeting: Helio Insurance - Procurement/Legal: retention terms + compliance reporting pack deliverables
Recorded: 2025-03-04 16:00 ET
Duration: 47 minutes
Participants:
- Markus Klein (Redwood)
- Sofia Mendes (Redwood Legal)
- Olga Petrov (Redwood GRC)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Product)
- Lauren Bishop (Helio Procurement)
- Samir Patel (Helio Legal)
- Mei Chen (Helio Security/Compliance)
- Jordan Alvarez (Helio IT Risk)

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for joining. The goal today is to go through the retention and compliance reporting pack items that came up in procurement. Lauren, Samir, you had some specific contract language questions.

[00:16] Lauren Bishop: Yep. Thank you Markus. We’re close, but we need the deliverables to be more explicit. Especially around what data you keep, for how long, and what you can produce on demand for audits.

[00:28] Samir Patel: And to be clear, we’re not trying to invent new obligations. We just need the agreement to reflect what your platform does, and what you’re committing to provide.

[00:39] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Sofia from our legal team is here. Olga is our GRC lead, and Naomi is the PM who owns the retention and reporting workstream.

[00:50] Mei Chen: Hi, everyone.

[00:52] Naomi Feldman: Hi.

[00:55] Sofia Mendes: Hello.

[00:58] Olga Petrov: Hi.

[01:00] Markus Klein: Great. Lauren, do you want to anchor on the two sections you flagged? I have the doc open but I may not have the latest redline.

[01:09] Lauren Bishop: Sure. First: “Retention Controls.” We need definitions: request logs, response logs, prompts and completions, audit logs, traces and metrics. Second: “Compliance Reporting Pack” as a named deliverable with timelines—like five business days, ten business days—whatever you can do, but stated.

[01:33] Samir Patel: Also “legal hold.” Your paper says you can support legal hold, but we need to understand what that actually means operationally. Is it a feature we can toggle, or a process, or both.

[01:46] Markus Klein: Yup. Naomi, do you want to give a quick overview of what’s included in the baseline reporting pack and retention controls as we’re shipping it?

[01:56] Naomi Feldman: Sure. So, retention controls is the productized ability for a customer admin to set retention periods—TTL—by data class. In the first release we’re focusing on (1) request/response logs where they’re stored, (2) audit logs, and (3) traces/metrics in our observability pipeline. We’ll have safe defaults by deployment tier—Hosted, Dedicated, Private—with min/max ranges. The compliance reporting pack is a generated package that includes: retention configuration export, audit log coverage summary, data residency/region summary, access control/RBAC summary, and an evidence checklist aligned to SOC2/ISO-style control themes.

[02:35] Jordan Alvarez: When you say “where they’re stored”—that’s important. Do you store prompts and completions by default?

[02:43] Markus Klein: Good question. It depends on logging configuration. We do not need to store prompts/completions to serve inference; it’s mostly for debugging and observability. Many customers choose to log metadata only. Naomi, want to clarify defaults?

[02:56] Naomi Feldman: For Hosted, default is limited request logging with a short retention, and we don’t store raw prompt/response content unless logging is enabled in a mode that includes content. For Dedicated and Private, we default to more restrictive settings—shorter retention and content logging off by default, unless the customer explicitly turns it on.

[03:18] Mei Chen: That aligns with what we want. But contractually, we need it to say that “content logging is optional and off by default,” or something like that.

[03:29] Sofia Mendes: We can work with that framing. We usually state it as: “Customer content is processed for the purpose of providing the services; Redwood does not retain customer content except as configured by the customer in the logging/telemetry settings.” We have to be careful to keep it true across deployment models.

[03:49] Samir Patel: Right. And if you retain content, it should be within the retention period configured, and then purged.

[03:56] Naomi Feldman: Yes—purged per TTL. And we can define purge semantics: deletions are performed via scheduled deletion jobs, idempotent, with verification metrics. There’s also exceptions like legal hold.

[04:10] Lauren Bishop: I’m going to be annoying here—what does “purged” mean? Is it immediate deletion at the TTL boundary? Or “best efforts within X days”?

[04:21] Markus Klein: Not annoying, that’s exactly the question.

[04:24] Naomi Feldman: Operationally it’s a scheduled process, so it’s not nanosecond-precise. We define an enforcement window. For example, data older than TTL is eligible for deletion, and then it’s deleted within a bounded lag. We track “TTL lag” as a metric.

[04:43] Jordan Alvarez: So we could ask for a maximum lag like 24 hours?

[04:47] Naomi Feldman: We’re cautious about promising a single number across all stores and regions today. In the product we alert if lag grows beyond thresholds; typical is hours, not weeks. But for contract language we can define it as “within a reasonable period” with a target, or “within X days,” depending on what you need.

[05:09] Samir Patel: We’ll propose language and you can counter. Our standard is deletion within 30 days of expiration, unless legal hold or incident response.

[05:20] Sofia Mendes: 30 days is generally workable as a contractual outer bound. We’ll confirm internally, but that’s in line with how many vendors do it.

[05:31] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Next: “Compliance Reporting Pack.” We need to know: is this an automated downloadable report? Or are we emailing you and you generate it manually?

[05:43] Markus Klein: Today it’s a product feature in progress; for early customers it may be partially assisted while the generator service is being finalized. The intent is on-demand generation via Console/API.

[05:57] Olga Petrov: For the baseline pack, what we commit is a standardized set of exports and summaries. Even if the first run is assisted, it’s the same artifact we’ll produce going forward. It’s meant to reduce the back-and-forth during security reviews.

[06:13] Mei Chen: What format? PDF? JSON? CSV?

[06:17] Olga Petrov: Likely a zipped package with a human-readable PDF summary plus machine-readable JSON/CSV exports for key tables—retention settings, audit log export, RBAC listing. The exact formats will be versioned.

[06:35] Samir Patel: We need the agreement to avoid “PDF only” because our auditors sometimes want raw exports.

[06:42] Olga Petrov: Understood. We can specify that the pack includes both human-readable and exportable data formats, subject to security constraints.

[06:55] Lauren Bishop: And timeline. You mentioned “on demand.” In practice, what are you willing to state? Five business days? Ten?

[07:05] Markus Klein: For the assisted path, we’ve been telling customers 5–10 business days depending on scope, and if it’s just a standard time window. For the automated path, it’s immediate.

[07:18] Naomi Feldman: Our MVP target is to make it self-serve for standard time windows and templates. For contractual language, we can commit that if self-serve is unavailable, Redwood will provide the report pack within, say, 10 business days of request.

[07:34] Samir Patel: That’s reasonable. Add “subject to customer providing required identifiers” or something.

[07:41] Sofia Mendes: Yes. We’ll define what constitutes a complete request—tenant ID, time window, and authorized requestor. That also ties into access controls.

[07:52] Jordan Alvarez: For access controls—can you include SSO/SAML details? Or is it just RBAC roles?

[07:59] Olga Petrov: Baseline pack includes RBAC summary and access control configuration summary—e.g., SSO enabled, domain restrictions, admin roles, and audit-log evidence of changes. We can’t always include full IdP logs because that’s outside Redwood, but we can show Redwood-side settings.

[08:21] Mei Chen: Audit logs, yes. We had an issue with a different vendor—missing event types. Can you confirm your audit log coverage?

[08:31] Markus Klein: We can share the event-type list and what’s in the export templates. We’ve recently improved time-windowed exports and filters.

[08:41] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs cover actions like: policy changes, role changes, API key creation, login events (where applicable), and report pack generation. The pack includes an “audit-log coverage summary,” which is basically a mapping of required control evidence to event types.

[09:06] Samir Patel: That’s the kind of thing we want explicitly named.

[09:10] Lauren Bishop: Also data residency. We need a region summary: what region our data is in, and confirmation it doesn’t leave.

[09:18] Markus Klein: For Dedicated/Private, we can pin region. For Hosted, it depends on selected region but we can provide a statement. Naomi?

[09:28] Naomi Feldman: The pack includes: configured region, where logs are stored, and for Dedicated/Private, the deployment’s residency configuration. For Private, you own the infra so it’s more like we describe what components store data and where you have placed them.

[09:49] Jordan Alvarez: We are leaning Dedicated first, not fully Private. But we need option to move to Private later.

[09:56] Markus Klein: That’s consistent with what we’ve seen.

[10:00] Mei Chen: Back to retention controls. You said “min/max by tier.” Can we set audit logs to 1 year?

[10:08] Naomi Feldman: For audit logs, we generally support longer retention because that’s needed for compliance. For request/response logs, we typically encourage shorter. The exact max TTL depends on tier and storage. Dedicated can do 365 days for audit logs, yes, subject to contract and cost.

[10:28] Lauren Bishop: Cost. Is longer retention a paid add-on?

[10:33] Markus Klein: Typically, yes, because storage and query costs go up. But we can price it as part of the Dedicated package. We’d rather make it explicit than bury it.

[10:46] Samir Patel: Contract should say retention is configurable “up to agreed limits,” and those limits can be in an order form.

[10:54] Sofia Mendes: Exactly. We can keep the MSA general and put specifics—like 365 days audit logs—in the order form or security addendum.

[11:05] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Now legal hold. We want the ability to stop deletion if there’s litigation.

[11:13] Samir Patel: And also incident hold, sometimes regulators ask to preserve logs.

[11:18] Naomi Feldman: Our design is: legal hold is an exception state that overrides TTL deletion for specified tenants and data classes. For Hosted/Dedicated, it’s a controlled process requiring approval. For Private, it could be self-managed depending on deployment.

[11:37] Mei Chen: So it’s not just a button in the UI today.

[11:41] Naomi Feldman: Not in the very first release. It’s an operational control with an audit trail. The key is it’s tracked and auditable.

[11:52] Sofia Mendes: From a contract standpoint, we can say Redwood will support legal hold requests and will not delete covered data while a hold is in effect, subject to authentication and scope.

[12:05] Samir Patel: We’ll need to define who can request it.

[12:09] Sofia Mendes: Yes, “Authorized Customer Representative,” named roles, etc.

[12:14] Lauren Bishop: Can you commit to a response time to place a hold? Like 24 hours?

[12:20] Markus Klein: I don’t want to overpromise. Naomi, what’s realistic?

[12:25] Naomi Feldman: For enterprise accounts, we can target one business day to acknowledge and begin processing. Actual placement depends on scope and store. But we can likely agree to “within 2 business days” to apply hold for standard stores.

[12:43] Olga Petrov: And the evidence pack can include confirmation that a hold was applied, with timestamps and approving actor.

[12:51] Jordan Alvarez: That’s good.

[12:54] Mei Chen: Another thing—purge verification. We don’t need your internal metrics, but we do want assurance there’s monitoring.

[13:03] Naomi Feldman: We do have metrics like TTL lag seconds, purge rows deleted, purge failures. We can include an “enforcement verification summary” in the pack, like a statement that deletion jobs are running and the lag was within thresholds for the requested period. We’re cautious about sharing raw internal dashboards, but we can include the relevant evidence.

[13:29] Samir Patel: That’s acceptable.

[13:32] Lauren Bishop: Switching gears: definitions. You used “request logs” and “audit logs” interchangeably earlier. We need clear definitions so we don’t have misunderstandings.

[13:43] Markus Klein: Totally. Let’s define now verbally, and we’ll align the doc.

[13:48] Naomi Feldman: Request/response logs: records of inference API calls—timestamps, model, token counts, latency, and optionally prompt/response content depending on logging mode. Audit logs: records of administrative actions in the platform—config changes, user/admin actions, access changes, report exports.

[14:12] Mei Chen: Good.

[14:13] Jordan Alvarez: Traces and metrics?

[14:16] Naomi Feldman: Observability telemetry about system behavior—latency histograms, error rates, tracing spans. Usually not customer content, but can include identifiers.

[14:30] Samir Patel: We’ll want the agreement to be explicit that “audit logs” are retained longer, and request logs shorter, unless configured.

[14:39] Sofia Mendes: We can do “default retention periods” in an exhibit, and then note they can be changed by the customer within permitted bounds.

[14:50] Lauren Bishop: And does Helio get to set those in a UI?

[14:54] Markus Klein: Yes, in the Redwood Console for Hosted/Dedicated. For Private, it can also be configured via Terraform or deployment config depending on the module.

[15:05] Mei Chen: We’ll be Dedicated, so UI is fine.

[15:09] Lauren Bishop: Now, compliance reporting pack. Is this the same as a SOC2 report?

[15:15] Olga Petrov: No. It’s not an attestation. It’s an evidence package about your tenant’s configuration and activity—things auditors ask for during your audit, plus internal audit support. Separately, we can provide our own SOC 2 report under NDA when available.

[15:32] Mei Chen: That’s what I expected.

[15:35] Samir Patel: But you’re not promising compliance.

[15:38] Sofia Mendes: Correct, we don’t promise that a report pack makes anyone compliant. We promise the artifact and the features.

[15:46] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Procurement wants it named as a deliverable to avoid “we’ll try to help.”

[15:54] Markus Klein: Understood.

[16:00] Mei Chen: What about report frequency? We might ask quarterly.

[16:05] Olga Petrov: That’s common. The pack can be generated per request. We can suggest cadence, but it’s on-demand.

[16:15] Jordan Alvarez: Any limits? Like only once a month?

[16:18] Markus Klein: There may be rate limits if it’s expensive, but for enterprise, it’s typically reasonable. If you need guaranteed frequency, we can include it.

[16:30] Lauren Bishop: Let’s keep it “on-demand, reasonable use,” unless legal needs a hard number.

[16:36] Samir Patel: I don’t need a hard number; I need a response SLA. Ten business days is fine.

[16:44] Markus Klein: Great.

[16:46] Naomi Feldman: Also, we should clarify what is in MVP vs later. MVP includes: retention config export, audit log export with filters and time windows, data residency summary, RBAC summary, and evidence checklist. Not included in MVP: fully custom report builder or deep integrations into GRC tooling.

[17:10] Mei Chen: That’s okay.

[17:12] Jordan Alvarez: Can the audit log export include a filter for “admin actions only”?

[17:17] Olga Petrov: Yes, by actor type and event category.

[17:21] Markus Klein: And time-windowed exports.

[17:24] Mei Chen: Perfect.

[17:26] Lauren Bishop: One more procurement point—if the report pack is a “manual effort,” we don’t want an open-ended professional services clause.

[17:36] Markus Klein: Totally fair. It’s intended to be part of the product entitlement. If we have to assist, it’s still included.

[17:44] Sofia Mendes: We’ll avoid calling it “professional services.” We’ll phrase it as “Support will provide the report pack within X business days upon request” until self-serve is available.

[17:56] Samir Patel: Great.

[18:00] Mei Chen: What about confidentiality in the report pack? It includes our settings and logs.

[18:06] Sofia Mendes: It would be treated as your confidential information. Delivery is via secure channel; access controlled. Also, we’ll log that it was generated and by whom.

[18:18] Jordan Alvarez: That last piece is good for audit trail.

[18:22] Markus Klein: Any other contract sections you want to hit?

[18:26] Samir Patel: Data deletion upon termination. If we terminate, do you delete everything within a period? And does legal hold override that?

[18:36] Sofia Mendes: Standard: we delete or return customer data within an agreed period after termination, subject to legal requirements and holds. Holds would override deletion for that scoped data if legally required.

[18:50] Lauren Bishop: Put numbers in there. We usually do 30–60 days.

[18:55] Sofia Mendes: We can align on 60 days post-termination for deletion of stored data, again with exceptions for legal hold and backups. We’ll craft language.

[19:09] Mei Chen: Backups—how does TTL work with backups?

[19:13] Naomi Feldman: Great question. TTL applies to primary stores; backups have their own lifecycle. Typically we can’t delete a specific record from an immutable backup, but backups roll off on their own schedule. We should be explicit about that.

[19:28] Samir Patel: Exactly. Contract should reflect that.

[19:31] Sofia Mendes: We’ll add a standard backup exception: data may persist in backups for a limited period, and is not used for production access.

[19:42] Jordan Alvarez: That’s fine.

[19:44] Markus Klein: On the product side, anything else you want confirmed, Mei?

[19:49] Mei Chen: Just want the event-type list for audit logs and the sample report pack. Our auditors are picky.

[19:56] Olga Petrov: We can send a sample pack with dummy data plus a coverage table.

[20:02] Mei Chen: Great.

[20:04] Lauren Bishop: And you’ll include the timeline in writing.

[20:07] Markus Klein: Yes.

[20:10] (crosstalk)

[20:11] Samir Patel: One more clause—limitations of liability. If you fail to delete on time, we want that treated as a security incident.

[20:21] Sofia Mendes: That’s tricky. A deletion delay is not necessarily unauthorized access. It may be a breach of contract, but not always a security incident. We can define it as a service failure and include notification if it materially impacts agreed retention.

[20:41] Mei Chen: Notification would help.

[20:44] Lauren Bishop: We don’t need it called a breach, but we need some remedy.

[20:48] Sofia Mendes: Understood. We can propose: if Redwood identifies a material failure to enforce configured retention beyond the contractual window, Redwood will notify Customer and remediate, and provide an incident report-like summary.

[21:07] Samir Patel: That’s closer.

[21:10] Markus Klein: And from engineering we have monitoring so we should detect issues.

[21:15] Naomi Feldman: We also have dashboards/alerts for TTL lag and purge failures. That’s how we avoid surprises.

[21:24] Jordan Alvarez: Can you include in the report pack any proof that those monitors exist?

[21:29] Olga Petrov: We can include a statement and evidence references. We won’t share internal pager configs, but we can show that verification is in place.

[21:40] Mei Chen: Works.

[21:42] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about delivery mechanism. Lauren, do you want it through a portal?

[21:48] Lauren Bishop: Ideally, yes. But if you have a secure link, okay. Our policy is no email attachments with sensitive data.

[21:56] Markus Klein: Understood. We can deliver via secure download link with access control, or through the console when self-serve is live.

[22:05] Sofia Mendes: We can specify “secure electronic delivery.”

[22:10] Samir Patel: Great.

[22:12] Naomi Feldman: On timing—Helio’s timeline: when do you need this by? For procurement.

[22:19] Lauren Bishop: We’re trying to close contract this month. But the report pack can be delivered during pilot as long as it’s committed.

[22:28] Mei Chen: Our audit is in Q3. We need the pack available well before then.

[22:34] Markus Klein: That’s doable.

[22:36] Naomi Feldman: MVP should be available ahead of that. We can commit to providing the pack on request during pilot, and then self-serve later.

[22:47] Jordan Alvarez: Can you commit to an ETA in the order form? Like “by June 30”?

[22:52] Markus Klein: Let’s be careful. We can commit to the deliverable as “available during pilot with support-assisted generation.” The self-serve generator date is roadmap. Sofia will probably advise against hard product dates.

[23:06] Sofia Mendes: Yes, we generally avoid roadmap dates in contracts. But we can commit to the deliverable SLA regardless of automation status.

[23:16] Samir Patel: That’s fine.

[23:19] Mei Chen: As long as it’s not “best effort.”

[23:22] Markus Klein: It won’t be.

[23:24] Olga Petrov: We’ll define the baseline contents so there’s no ambiguity.

[23:30] Lauren Bishop: Great. Do you have a list of what’s included? Like bullet points.

[23:35] Olga Petrov: Yes. I’ll send after this call: (1) audit-log export summary with time window and filters, (2) retention configuration export and change history, (3) data residency/region configuration summary, (4) RBAC/access control report, (5) evidence checklist mapping.

[23:57] Mei Chen: Include “report generation is itself audited.”

[24:02] Olga Petrov: Yes—good call.

[24:05] Markus Klein: Anything else from Helio legal?

[24:09] Samir Patel: One last item: subcontractors. If your audit-log exporter or analytics uses third parties, we need that in the DPA.

[24:18] Sofia Mendes: We have a subprocessors list in the DPA. For the report pack, it’s generated from our systems. If any subprocessor is involved in storage or delivery, it’ll be listed. We can confirm if the delivery uses our own infrastructure.

[24:35] Lauren Bishop: Okay.

[24:36] Mei Chen: And encryption at rest, KMS?

[24:40] Markus Klein: Dedicated supports customer-managed keys in certain configurations, and Private definitely does. Hosted uses Redwood-managed KMS.

[24:50] Mei Chen: We’ll stick with Redwood-managed for now.

[24:54] Markus Klein: Sounds good.

[25:00] (brief silence)

[25:01] Markus Klein: Let me recap what I heard, and please correct me.

[25:06] Markus Klein: One: Update contract language to define data classes—request/response logs, audit logs, traces/metrics—and state content logging is optional/off by default. Two: Add deletion semantics: eligible at TTL, deleted within a bounded window (we’ll propose 30 days). Three: Add legal hold / incident hold process with response targets and audit trail. Four: Name the compliance reporting pack deliverable, include contents list and delivery SLA (10 business days if not self-serve). Five: Provide sample report pack and audit event coverage list this week.

[25:46] Lauren Bishop: That’s right.

[25:48] Samir Patel: Yes.

[25:50] Mei Chen: Yes, plus the secure delivery point.

[25:53] Markus Klein: Yep—secure electronic delivery.

[25:56] Naomi Feldman: Also clarify backups retention exception.

[25:59] Sofia Mendes: Yes.

[26:01] Jordan Alvarez: And delete after termination window.

[26:04] Sofia Mendes: Noted.

[26:06] Markus Klein: Great. We can end early unless there are more questions.

[26:12] Lauren Bishop: I have one. Can you confirm that in Dedicated our data is isolated? Like no co-mingling.

[26:19] Markus Klein: Yes, dedicated capacity with isolation. The retention and audit logs are scoped per tenant. Naomi might add that config is per tenant.

[26:28] Naomi Feldman: Correct.

[26:31] Mei Chen: Okay.

[26:33] Samir Patel: Alright, we’ll send redlines. Thank you.

[26:38] Markus Klein: Thanks all. Olga, Sofia, Naomi—we’ll follow up with the docs.

[26:44] Olga Petrov: Thanks.

[26:45] Sofia Mendes: Thank you.

[26:46] Naomi Feldman: Thanks.

---
Notes: Call ended a bit early; remaining time in calendar was unused.
